paragraphs: This paper introduces a Markov chain Monte Carlo method for posterior sampling in Bayesian nonparametric mixture models. It targets models whose priors belong to the Poisson-Kingman class. The central computational issue is how to represent the model’s infinite-dimensional component while running a sampling procedure with practical memory and storage requirements.

The proposed sampler uses a compact representation of that infinite component. The authors emphasize that it remains explicitly represented while requiring less memory and storage than previous MCMC schemes. This is the main methodological contribution: changing how the sampler represents part of the model to reduce the resources needed for posterior computation.

The paper compares the method with existing marginal and conditional MCMC samplers through simulations. These comparisons demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm in the evaluated settings. Together, the representation and simulation results offer a way to make sampling within this general prior family more economical, with the stated resource advantage specifically concerning memory and storage.
neurips-2015-a-hybrid-sampler-for-poisso.tldr: A compact representation of Poisson-Kingman mixture models enables posterior sampling with lower memory and storage requirements than previous MCMC schemes.

paragraphs: Robust principal component analysis seeks to separate an observed matrix into a low-rank component and a sparse matrix of errors. This paper studies when Principal Component Pursuit, a convex optimization approach to that separation, can recover the correct components. Its focus is on how the locations of errors affect recovery.

Earlier analyses assumed that entries were corrupted through uniform Bernoulli sampling, giving each entry the same corruption probability. The authors allow those probabilities to differ. They derive conditions for individual entries using the low-rank matrix’s local incoherence, relating the tolerated corruption pattern to the matrix’s structure at each location.

The resulting guarantee is conditional: Principal Component Pursuit correctly separates the matrices when the specified entry-level corruption conditions hold. This provides a more detailed account of robustness than a uniform corruption model. To establish it, the proof introduces a weighted norm and develops its concentration properties, supplying mathematical tools for analyzing unequal corruption probabilities.
neurips-2015-analysis-of-robust-pca-via-.tldr: An entry-level analysis gives recovery guarantees for robust PCA when matrix entries have unequal probabilities of corruption.

paragraphs: Asynchronous stochastic gradient methods allow multiple workers to contribute to optimization without proceeding in synchronized rounds. Such implementations had achieved practical success in deep learning, but existing theory did not adequately explain their convergence or speedup for nonconvex objectives. This paper addresses that theoretical gap.

The authors analyze two implementations: one operating across a computer network and another using shared memory. For both, they establish an ergodic convergence rate of O(1/√K), where K is the total number of iterations. The ergodic qualification concerns an aggregate convergence measure across iterations, rather than asserting the same progress for every individual update.

They also show that linear speedup is achievable when the number of workers is bounded by √K. This makes the parallelism claim conditional on the relationship between worker count and iteration count. The results extend and improve earlier convex analyses, providing theoretical support for asynchronous computation in the nonconvex setting that motivates deep learning applications.
neurips-2015-asynchronous-parallel-stoch.tldr: Two asynchronous stochastic gradient implementations receive nonconvex convergence guarantees and conditional linear-speedup results.

paragraphs: BinaryConnect explores whether neural networks can train effectively while using weights restricted to two possible values during computation. The motivation is hardware efficiency: binary weights could replace many multiply-and-accumulate operations with simpler accumulations. Multipliers consume substantial space and power in digital neural-network implementations, making this change attractive for specialized hardware.

The method uses binary weights in both forward and backward propagation. It nevertheless retains higher precision in the stored weights where gradient updates accumulate. This distinction is central to the approach: the weights used for propagation have two values, while the underlying training state preserves more detailed updates.

The authors show that BinaryConnect also acts as a regularizer, drawing a connection to dropout-style methods. They report near-state-of-the-art results on permutation-invariant MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN. These findings demonstrate that the propagation constraint can coexist with strong predictive performance on the evaluated tasks, while the hardware discussion identifies why such a constraint could be computationally valuable.
neurips-2015-binaryconnect-training-deep.tldr: BinaryConnect trains with binary propagation weights and higher-precision stored updates, achieving near-state-of-the-art results on three image benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization objectives that sum many component functions, with iterates projected onto a convex parameter set. The target regime has far more component functions than parameters, while the parameter dimension is itself large. In this setting, processing only a subset of the components can reduce computational work.

The authors combine subsampling with a low-rank approximation to construct a randomized batch algorithm. They report a convergence rate comparable to Newton’s method with substantially lower cost per iteration. The stated convergence behavior is composite: quadratic progress at the start, followed by linear convergence when the iterate is close to the minimizer.

The analysis also supports selecting near-optimal algorithm parameters, and the algorithm is described as robust to the starting point and step size. Beyond the new method, the theoretical results can supply convergence rates for earlier subsampling algorithms. The paper connects the analysis to established machine learning problems and evaluates the proposed method across several datasets and scenarios.
neurips-2015-convergence-rates-of-sub-sa.tldr: Subsampling and low-rank approximation yield a cheaper Newton-like algorithm with analyzed quadratic-then-linear convergence.

paragraphs: This paper studies restless bandits whose arms produce rewards through stationary φ-mixing processes. Rewards are dependent across time, so collecting another observation does not necessarily provide the independence that ordinary bandit reasoning relies on. The learning problem therefore includes managing dependence alongside choosing which arms to explore and exploit.

The proposed Remix-UCB algorithm introduces a waiting arm and deliberately ignores some reward values to recover useful independence. It generalizes Improved-UCB to this dependent setting. Waiting becomes part of the decision process because the value of an observation depends partly on its temporal relationship to other observations.

The authors provide a regret analysis with two notable properties. When all mixing coefficients are zero, the method reduces to Improved-UCB in the independent setting. When dependence decays as φ(n) = O(n^−α), the analysis gives controlled regret depending on the horizon, decay rate, and gap between the best and next-best arms. The result also covers α below one, where the mixing coefficients are not summable.
neurips-2015-cornering-stationary-and-re.tldr: Remix-UCB uses waiting to manage dependent bandit rewards and provides regret guarantees even for some slowly mixing processes.

paragraphs: Adaptive learning rates adjust update sizes separately for different parameters, helping address ill-conditioning in large neural networks. This paper asks how those adjustments should account for nonconvex curvature. Its motivation comes from research suggesting that many critical points encountered during network training are saddle points, where curvature can have both positive and negative directions.

The authors show that the Jacobi preconditioner can behave undesirably when those curvature signs coexist. They present theoretical and empirical evidence favoring an equilibration preconditioner for nonconvex problems. They then use that preconditioner to develop ESGD, a new scheme for adapting learning rates.

In the reported experiments, ESGD and RMSProp produce very similar update directions, while ESGD sometimes converges faster. ESGD also clearly improves on plain stochastic gradient descent throughout those experiments. The findings support accounting for mixed-sign curvature when designing adaptive updates, with the speed advantage over RMSProp remaining an empirical result that occurs in some evaluated cases.
neurips-2015-equilibrated-adaptive-learn.tldr: ESGD adapts learning rates through equilibration, with evidence that this handles nonconvex curvature better than Jacobi preconditioning.

paragraphs: Biclustering searches a high-dimensional dataset for a notable submatrix: a selected group of rows together with a selected group of columns. This paper addresses how to assess the statistical significance of a bicluster after an algorithm has found it. The challenge is that the same data guided the selection of the pattern being tested.

The authors develop an inference framework for biclusters chosen by score-based algorithms. They treat the problem as selective inference, meaning the statistical assessment accounts for the data-dependent selection. This connects the discovery step to the subsequent uncertainty calculation instead of treating the selected submatrix as though it had been specified independently.

The framework provides exact confidence intervals and p-values for the selected biclusters. Here, exactness is non-asymptotic: the stated result does not rely on taking a large-sample limit. The authors also extend their approach to exact inference for Gaussian statistics. The contribution supplies inferential tools for interpreting discovered structures, complementing the algorithms that locate them.
neurips-2015-evaluating-the-statistical-.tldr: A selective-inference framework gives exact confidence intervals and p-values for biclusters chosen by score-based algorithms.

paragraphs: Tensor CP decomposition is used in latent-variable learning and data mining, but its computations can be expensive. This paper develops randomized decomposition algorithms based on sketches: compact computational representations built using hashing. The authors start from count sketches and introduce techniques tailored to tensor operations.

A central contribution is computing randomized tensor contractions with fast Fourier transforms without explicitly constructing the tensors. These contractions appear in tensor power iterations and alternating least squares. The paper also introduces colliding hashes for symmetric tensors, reducing the time required to compute their sketches.

Combining these ideas with whitening and tensor power iteration yields what the authors describe as the fastest algorithm for both sparse and dense tensors. They state that approximation quality does not depend on properties such as sparsity or uniformity of tensor entries. An application to topic modeling gives competitive results. The contribution thus joins faster core computations with an approximation guarantee that is not tied to those particular tensor characteristics.
neurips-2015-fast-and-guaranteed-tensor-.tldr: Tensor-specific sketches accelerate CP decomposition by computing key contractions without explicitly forming tensors.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning infers reward functions from an expert’s demonstrated behavior. This paper relaxes the assumption that an entire demonstrated trajectory follows a single reward function. It instead allows multiple reward functions to explain different locally consistent portions of one trajectory, accommodating behavior whose underlying objectives change along the way.

The learning task includes both the reward functions and the probabilities of switching between them at any state, including states absent from the demonstrations. The authors express this task as a probabilistic graphical model. An expectation-maximization algorithm then iteratively updates the rewards and switching behavior to jointly improve the likelihood of the demonstrated trajectories.

The fitted model also provides a most likely division of a trajectory into segments associated with different rewards. On synthetic and real-world datasets, the method outperforms EM clustering combined with maximum-likelihood inverse reinforcement learning. The authors show that this comparison method is a reduced version of their approach, connecting the empirical result to the broader formulation.
neurips-2015-inverse-reinforcement-learn.tldr: A graphical-model approach learns multiple reward functions and their switching probabilities within individual expert trajectories.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether influence functions in networks can be learned from observed cascades. It establishes probably approximately correct learnability for three common models: Linear Threshold, Independent Cascade, and Voter. It also provides sample-complexity results for each, addressing how much observational data learning requires within that framework.

The proofs use different mathematical connections for the three models. Linear Threshold influence is related to neural networks. Independent Cascade influence is expressed as an expectation over randomly drawn subgraphs and analyzed with covering-number arguments. For the Voter model, the learning problem is reduced to linear regression.

The learnability results hold when cascades are only partially observed and the times at which nodes become influenced are unavailable. Separately, the authors provide efficient polynomial-time learning algorithms for fully observed cascades that include those times. This distinction matters: the abstract establishes statistical learnability with less information, while its efficient algorithmic results concern the richer observation setting.
neurips-2015-learnability-of-influence-i.tldr: Influence functions are PAC-learnable in three network models, with efficient algorithms additionally provided for fully observed cascades.

paragraphs: This paper develops learning guarantees for forecasting time series whose statistical behavior can change over time. It considers non-stationary, non-mixing stochastic processes, a general setting that allows both distributional change and dependence that need not satisfy a mixing condition. The aim is to ground forecasting algorithms in theory suited to that setting.

The bounds depend on a data-dependent measure of sequential complexity and a discrepancy measure. These quantities organize the guarantee around the complexity of sequential prediction and the discrepancy relevant to learning from changing data. The authors state that the discrepancy can be estimated from observations under mild assumptions, making that part of the guarantee accessible from data.

The authors then use the bounds to design forecasting algorithms for non-stationary time series. They report preliminary experimental results for these algorithms. The contribution therefore connects a general theoretical formulation to algorithm design, while the empirical evidence is explicitly early-stage. The stated estimability of discrepancy also remains conditional on the assumptions identified by the authors.
neurips-2015-learning-theory-and-algorit.tldr: Data-dependent learning bounds guide forecasting algorithms for time series that may be non-stationary and non-mixing.

paragraphs: This paper examines binary classification when labels are corrupted by symmetric noise. A previous theoretical result showed that minimizing convex potentials over linear functions can yield classification performance equivalent to random guessing under this noise. The authors investigate whether a carefully chosen convex loss can nevertheless be robust.

They introduce the unhinged loss by modifying hinge loss so that it is no longer clamped at zero. The resulting loss can decrease without a finite lower bound. This property allows it to avoid the earlier impossibility result. The authors prove that the loss is classification-calibrated and robust to symmetric label noise.

The paper also connects the optimal unhinged solution to a strongly regularized support vector machine and to limiting solutions for convex potentials. From these relationships, the authors conclude that strong l2 regularization makes most standard learners robust to symmetric label noise. Experiments support the unhinged loss’s robustness. The result concerns this particular noise model, with the unusual loss shape explaining how convexity remains compatible with robustness.
neurips-2015-learning-with-symmetric-lab.tldr: The negatively unbounded unhinged loss is convex and robust to symmetric label noise, with connections to strong l2 regularization.

paragraphs: Mean field variational Bayes is attractive for posterior approximation because it runs quickly on large datasets. Its uncertainty estimates can be much less reliable: it may substantially underestimate uncertainty in individual variables and supplies no information about covariance between variables. This paper addresses those weaknesses in uncertainty estimation.

The authors adapt linear response methods from statistical physics and call the resulting approach linear response variational Bayes. LRVB aims to estimate both individual-variable uncertainty and the way variables vary together. Its purpose is to provide a coherent covariance estimate alongside the computationally convenient mean field approximation.

When the mean field approximation belongs to the exponential family, LRVB takes a simple analytic form, including for non-conjugate models. This condition applies to the approximation; the authors impose no assumption on the form of the true posterior. Experiments across models using simulated and real data demonstrate accuracy and scalability, supporting the method as a way to improve uncertainty estimates obtained from mean field inference.
neurips-2015-linear-response-methods-for.tldr: Linear response variational Bayes improves variance and covariance estimates derived from mean field posterior approximations.

paragraphs: This paper considers how to produce several good but different labelings in a graphical model. A sequential approach selects one solution after another, making each choice greedily. Joint inference chooses all M solutions together. Earlier work had shown that joint solutions could have lower total energy and better qualitative results, but their computational cost hindered use.

The authors show that the joint problem can be expressed as submodular energy minimization when the original maximum a posteriori inference problem is submodular. This preserves a useful optimization structure while asking for several diverse answers. Consequently, fast methods for submodular minimization can be applied to the joint inference task.

The paper also presents practical algorithms that outperform the current state of the art and apply to both submodular and non-submodular cases. The theoretical reformulation remains conditional on submodularity of the original problem. The broader practical algorithms extend the paper’s reach beyond that condition, addressing the computational obstacle that made joint selection difficult to use.
neurips-2015-m-best-diverse-labelings-fo.tldr: Jointly finding diverse labelings becomes submodular optimization when the original inference problem is submodular, enabling faster inference.

paragraphs: This paper studies the welfare of outcomes produced by no-regret learning when players have private information. Earlier price-of-anarchy analyses connected such learning to near-optimal welfare in complete-information games. The authors extend that connection to Bayesian games, where some information relevant to play is not publicly known.

The first result transfers a welfare guarantee through a specific proof structure. If near-optimal welfare in the corresponding public-information game is established using smoothness, that proof directly implies near-optimal welfare in the Bayesian game. The guarantee therefore rests on the availability of that smoothness-based argument for the underlying game.

The second result shows that no-regret learning dynamics converge to Bayesian coarse correlated equilibrium. This connects the welfare analysis to outcomes reached through learning under incomplete information. Both results use an interpretation of a Bayesian game as a stochastic complete-information game. Together, they provide a route from existing welfare proofs to guarantees for learning behavior when information is private.
neurips-2015-no-regret-learning-in-bayes.tldr: Smoothness-based welfare guarantees extend to Bayesian games, where no-regret dynamics converge to Bayesian coarse correlated equilibrium.

paragraphs: Log-linear models need a normalizing calculation to turn their scores into probabilities, and this can be expensive when there are many possible outputs. Self-normalization addresses that cost by penalizing deviations of the log-normalizer from zero during training. This allows unnormalized scores to serve as approximate probabilities.

The paper analyzes the accuracy consequences of this technique, whose practical effectiveness had outpaced its theoretical explanation. The authors prove upper bounds on the accuracy loss caused by self-normalization. They also identify input-distribution classes that are easy to self-normalize and construct explicit examples of high-variance input distributions.

These results yield predictions about how difficult it will be to fit self-normalized models to different distribution classes. The authors validate those predictions with real and synthetic datasets. The contribution gives theoretical structure to the computational tradeoff: simplifying probability calculation has an accuracy cost that can be bounded, and the suitability of the approach depends on properties of the input distribution.
neurips-2015-on-the-accuracy-of-self-nor.tldr: The paper bounds accuracy losses from self-normalization and explains how input distributions affect its suitability.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimation when an observation depends on a linear combination of inputs through an unknown transformation. That transformation may be noisy, nonlinear, noninvertible, or reduced to a single bit. The resulting single-index model substantially broadens ordinary linear regression and includes a generalization of one-bit compressed sensing.

The authors propose a spectral estimation procedure that can recover the model parameter for classes of link functions where previous algorithms fail. They describe the restrictions on the unknown relationship as mild. For the high-dimensional case, where parameters outnumber observations, they assume a sparse parameter and introduce a two-stage nonconvex estimation framework.

The paper also establishes minimax lower bounds for a broad class of link functions. These demonstrate the optimality of the proposed estimators in both classical and high-dimensional regimes. The significance is that unknown nonlinear observation mechanisms need not prevent optimal estimation within the analyzed classes, including settings where sparsity is used to address limited observations.
neurips-2015-optimal-linear-estimation-u.tldr: Spectral and two-stage nonconvex estimators recover linear parameters through broad classes of unknown nonlinear observation functions with optimality guarantees.

paragraphs: Large datasets make conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo expensive for Bayesian inference. Embarrassingly parallel MCMC distributes the work by splitting the data, running independent samplers on the subsets, and combining their posterior draws. The combination step determines the final approximation and can create difficulties for accuracy and subsequent resampling.

The proposed PART algorithm uses random partition trees to combine the subset draws. The authors describe this construction as distribution-free, adaptable to multiple scales, and easy to resample from. These properties target both the quality of the combined approximation and the practical ability to generate draws from it.

The paper supplies theoretical justification and extensive experiments illustrating empirical performance. Its central contribution is therefore a new aggregation mechanism within the parallel sampling workflow. Independent subset sampling already provides the division of computational labor; PART addresses how the resulting samples can be brought together into a usable final approximation while tackling the shortcomings identified in existing combining methods.
neurips-2015-parallelizing-mcmc-with-ran.tldr: PART combines independently sampled subset posteriors using random partition trees to improve aggregation and simplify resampling.

paragraphs: Estimating a graphical model’s partition function presents a tradeoff between two inference approaches. Convex variational methods can give deterministic bounds, but those bounds may be loose and difficult to tighten through additional computation. Importance sampling can improve as more samples are collected, but its effectiveness depends strongly on its proposal distribution.

This paper combines the approaches by adding importance sampling to convex variational bounds. The authors argue that variational methods naturally supply proposals that cover the target distribution’s probability. They also reinterpret variational optimization as choosing a proposal that minimizes an upper bound on the sampling estimator’s variance.

The combination produces an accurate estimator and probabilistic bounds that can improve as computation continues. The authors report that these bounds quickly improve on state-of-the-art variational bounds. Accuracy certificates become available given enough samples relative to the initial bound’s error. This condition links the quality of the variational starting point to the sampling effort needed for a certified result.
neurips-2015-probabilistic-variational-b.tldr: Combining convex variational inference with importance sampling yields progressively tighter probabilistic bounds on graphical-model partition functions.

paragraphs: Gaussian graphical models are used to study network structure, including relationships in gene-expression and social-interaction data. In modern applications, the data may be high-dimensional and contain outliers or heavier tails than a Gaussian distribution. This paper develops a method for estimating sparse Gaussian graphical models in the presence of such challenges.

The proposed Trimmed Graphical Lasso uses an implicit trimming mechanism to guard against outliers. The authors relate this mechanism to Least Trimmed Squares in linear regression. Trimming is the organizing idea behind the estimator’s robustness, adapting an approach associated with regression to sparse network estimation.

The paper provides a rigorous statistical analysis in the high-dimensional setting, addressing a lack of statistical guarantees in existing robust sparse graphical-model approaches. Experiments with simulated data and real gene-expression data further demonstrate the method’s value. Together, the theory and evaluations support using trimming as a principled component of robust estimation when atypical observations can interfere with recovering network structure.
neurips-2015-robust-gaussian-graphical-m.tldr: Trimmed Graphical Lasso uses implicit trimming to robustly estimate sparse Gaussian graphical models, supported by high-dimensional statistical analysis.

paragraphs: A simple link-prediction heuristic ranks other nodes by how many neighbors they share with a query node. This rule is fast and works well in practice, while more theoretically established methods such as spectral clustering can be expensive on large graphs. The paper investigates whether shared-neighbor information also supports reliable cluster recovery.

The analysis uses stochastic blockmodels, a network formulation organized around groups of nodes. The authors show that the common-neighbors heuristic can extract clusters with high probability when the graph is sufficiently dense. They also show that adding a cleaning step permits recovery in sparser graphs.

Experiments on simulated and real-world data support these conclusions. The contribution provides theoretical backing for a computationally simple network heuristic and identifies density as a condition affecting its guarantees. The cleaning step extends the range of graphs covered by the result, connecting a practical refinement to improved recovery behavior in the analyzed model.
neurips-2015-the-consistency-of-common-n.tldr: Common-neighbor counts recover clusters with high probability in sufficiently dense stochastic blockmodels, with cleaning extending recovery to sparser graphs.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer flexible statistical models with automatically calibrated complexity, yet standard kernels can struggle to extend patterns that people extrapolate easily. This paper investigates what human responses to function-extrapolation problems reveal about the assumptions guiding that behavior. The goal is to capture some of those assumptions in learned kernels.

The authors create extrapolation tasks, collect human responses, and develop a kernel-learning framework across behavioral experiments. They use it to reverse engineer inductive biases: the preferences that guide predictions beyond the observed portion of a function. Learning from responses connects a mathematical modeling component to measured human behavior.

The resulting kernels are used both to gain psychological insight and to extrapolate in human-like ways beyond traditional stationary and polynomial kernels. The paper also investigates Occam’s razor in human and Gaussian-process function learning. Its contribution links model construction with behavioral analysis, using the same learned representation to explore how people generalize and to reproduce aspects of their predictions.
neurips-2015-the-human-kernel-cf2b18d7c6.tldr: Kernels learned from human extrapolation responses capture inductive biases and enable more human-like function predictions.

paragraphs: Visual analogy asks for an image that completes a relationship: image A relates to image B as image C relates to the missing image D. Solving it requires identifying the mapping between the first pair and finding a second pair that expresses a similar mapping. This paper formulates that task for natural images.

The authors learn an embedding using convolutional neural networks arranged in a quadruple Siamese architecture. The training objective encourages analogous image pairs with similar transformations to lie close together in the learned representation. The representation is therefore organized around relationships between images, which is the information needed to complete an analogy.

The paper also introduces a dataset of natural-image analogy questions and reports initial results on solving them. Its contribution combines a task formulation, a learning architecture, and data for evaluation. These first results establish an approach to the problem, showing how visual transformations can serve as the basis for searching for an image that completes a specified relationship.
neurips-2015-visalogy-answering-visual-a.tldr: A quadruple Siamese convolutional network learns relationships between image pairs to answer natural-image analogy questions.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes the Lovász theta function and its associated geometric embedding to graphs with weights on both nodes and edges. The aim is a shared mathematical construction for weighted graph problems. Including both kinds of weights allows the formulation to incorporate information attached to individual nodes as well as their connections.

The authors show that the generalized function can be computed exactly with semidefinite programming. They also provide an approximation route using support vector machine computations. These give two computational ways to access the proposed construction, distinguishing an exact optimization formulation from an approximate method.

The paper interprets the theta function as a measure of graph diversity. It uses that interpretation together with the embedding in algorithms for Max-Cut, correlation clustering, and document summarization. All three are represented as weighted graph problems. The contribution is a unifying representation and computational framework that carries a common notion of diversity into several different algorithmic tasks.
neurips-2015-weighted-theta-functions-an.tldr: A weighted generalization of the Lovász theta function supplies a diversity measure and embedding for graph optimization and summarization.
